IK-1841885:L60.text: J U D G M E N T (Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 20366/2002) ARIJIT PASAYAT,J Leave granted.

IK-1841885:L61.text: The appellants who were plaintiffs in a suit filed before the learned Civil Judge, Senior Division, Srirampur have questioned legality of the conclusions arrived at by the Courts below holding that the plaint filed by them was to be rejected in terms of cite11†Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure , 1908 (in short the 'Code'). The plaintiffs claimed to be tenants under respondent No.2, Shaneshwar Deosthan Trust (hereinafter referred to as the 'trust').

IK-1841885:L62.text: Its trustees and the Assistant Charity Commissioner (in short the 'Commissioner') were the other defendants. Plaintiffs claimed that they were tenants of the trust of which the defendants Nos. 3 to 13 were the trustees. Alleging that they have been forcibly evicted notwithstanding continuance of the tenancy, the suit was filed for the following reliefs:

IK-1841885:L63.text: > A) Plaintiff no. 1 to 17, be declared as the tenants of the properties described in the plaint belonging to temple Trust, of which defendant No.2 to 13 are trustees.

IK-1841885:L64.text: > B) Defendant No.1 to 13, be permanently restrained by an order of injunction not to evict plaintiff No.1 to 13, forcibly with the help of police and also not to interfere in their business being carried on by them in suit shops, and not to interfere in the possession of suit shops in any manner-whatsoever, either by themselves or by their servants, agents, relatives or anybody claiming through or under them.

IK-1841885:L65.text: > C) Direct the defendant No. 2 to 13, to pay compensation for the loss caused to the plaintiffs on account of their acts of omission and commission as described in the plaint, committed by them prior to the filing of the suit and during pendency of suit for the damage that may be caused to the plaintiffs.

IK-1841885:L67.text: > D) Defendant No.1 be directed to enquire into the illegal acts, committed by defendant No.2 to 13, and issue appropriate direction to that effect.

IK-1841885:L68.text: The suit was numbered as R.C.S. No.160/1997 in the trial Court. The stand of the plaintiffs-appellants essentially was that the tenancy was for a period of 11 years and not for 11 months as claimed by the trust. An application was filed by the trust raising a preliminary plea that the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code.

IK-1841885:L69.text: With reference to cite12†Section 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 (in short the 'Act') it was urged that no Civil court had jurisdiction to decide or deal with any question which by or under the Act is to be decided or dealt with by any officer or authority under the Act and in respect of which the decision or order of such officer or authority has been made final and conclusive. The trial Judge framed two preliminary issues, i.e.

IK-1841885:L70.text: (a) whether the suit was liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code for want of cause of action, and (b) whether the suit was tenable against all the defendants. Findings in respect of the preliminary issues were recorded against the plaintiffs.

IK-1841885:L71.text: A finding was recorded that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action and also in view of the specific provisions of the Act, the jurisdiction vests only with the District Court to give direction to Commissioner and in any event cite12†Section 80 of the Act took away jurisdiction of the Civil Court and the plaint was rejected.

IK-1841885:L72.text: Challenging the judgment and decree dated 21.10.2000 passed by the learned Civil Judge, Senior Division, Srirampur, an appeal was preferred before the District Court which was numbered as Regular Civil Appeal No.178 of 2000. The appeal was dismissed and the decree passed by the trial Court was confirmed by II Additional District Judge at Srirampur, Ahmed Nagar District.

IK-1841885:L73.text: The matter was carried in Second Appeal before the High Court which by the impugned judgment upheld the findings recorded by the Courts below. Before the High Court, it was contended by the appellants that cite13†Sections 50 , cite14†51 and cite12†80 of the Act had no application and the lease being for 11 years, the action of the trust in dispossessing the plaintiffs forcibly cannot have the approval of law.

IK-1841885:L74.text: The stand of the trust was to the effect that the plaintiffs have not approached the Court with clean hands. They had tried to get relief from the High Court by filing a petition under cite15†Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 (in short the 'Constitution'). They failed to comply with the interim directions given by the High Court and before the date posted before the High Court for consideration of the interim orders, they filed the suit and prayed for injunction.

IK-1841885:L75.text: Subsequently, the writ petition was withdrawn. The plaint filed by the plaintiffs did not disclose any cause of action and in any event the relief sought for could not have been granted by the Civil Court in view of the specific provisions contained in cite13†Sections 50 , cite14†51 and cite12†80 of the Act. There was no forcible dispossession as claimed. The Courts below were justified in rejecting the plaint.

IK-1841885:L76.text: The High Court accepted the plea of the trust and dismissed the second appeal affirming the conclusions arrived by the Courts below.

IK-1841885:L77.text: In support of the appeal, Mr. V.A. Mohta, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that the Courts below have lost sight of the nuances of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code. Even if for the sake of arguments it is conceded that some reliefs were to be dealt with by the authorities under the Act, the reliefs were severable and the Civil Court had jurisdiction to deal with them.

IK-1841885:L78.text: The dispute projected in the suit essentially related to the question of tenancy and the relationship between the plaintiffs and the defendant-trust vis-`-vis the question of tenancy, the term of tenancy are matters intermittently linked with these basic issues. Such issues cannot be decided by the authorities under the Act. Therefore, the rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code cannot be maintained in law.

IK-1841885:L79.text: The plaintiffs were dispossessed illegally and a person dispossessed illegally was entitled to protection. A person without title but in 'settled' possession as against mere fugitive possession, can get back possession if forcibly dispossessed or rather if dispossessed otherwise than by due process of law.

IK-1841885:L80.text: Per contra, Mr. A.V. Savant, learned senior counsel appearing for the defendant-trust submitted that the Courts below have concurrently found it as a matter of fact that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action and the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to deal with a matter, specifically in view of what has been statutorily provided in cite12†Section 80 of the Act. With reference to the judgment of the High court it was pointed out that the plaintiffs had not approached the Court with clean hands.

IK-1841885:L81.text: They had adopted dubious methods, did not comply with the directions of the High Court for depositing the stipulated amount. By a ruse, some reliefs have been sought for in the plaint totally out of context with the main prayers which are to be dealt with in terms of cite13†Sections 50 and cite14†51 of the Act. There were no pleadings about alleged forcible dis-possession and wholly untenable plea about the period of tenancy has been rightly rejected by the Courts below.

IK-1841885:L82.text: Clauses (a) and (d) of Rule 11 have full application to the facts of the case. The whole purpose in filing the suit was to somehow or other remains in possession of the shops which were leased out to them for certain periods. As a result of the actions of the plaintiffs, the trust would have been put to huge financial loss. All this according to him, disentitle the appellants from any relief under cite16†Article 136 of the Constitution.

IK-1841885:L83.text: Order VII Rule 11 of the Code reads as follows:

IK-1841885:L85.text: > Order VII Rule 11: Rejection of plaint.  The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases :-

IK-1841885:L87.text: > (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action;

IK-1841885:L89.text: > (b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so;

IK-1841885:L90.text: > (c) where the relief claims is properly valued but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

IK-1841885:L92.text: > (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law;

IK-1841885:L94.text: > (e) where it is not filed in duplicate;

IK-1841885:L96.text: > (f) where the plaintiff fails to comply with the provisions of rule 9.

IK-1841885:L97.text: Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not be extended unless the Court, for reasons to be recorded, is satisfied that the plaintiff was prevented by any cause of an exceptional nature for correcting the valuation or supplying the requisite stamp- paper, as the case may be, within the time fixed by the Court and that refusal to extend such time would cause grave injustice to the plaintiff."

IK-1841885:L98.text: In the present case the respondent-trust has relied upon clauses (a) and (d) of Rule 11.

IK-1841885:L100.text: Before dealing with the factual scenario, the spectrum of Order VII Rule 11 in the legal ambit needs to be noted.

IK-1841885:L101.text: In cite17†Saleem Bhai and Ors. v. State of Maharashtra and Ors. (2003 (1) SCC 557) it was held with reference to Order VII Rule 11 of the Code that the relevant facts which need to be looked into for deciding an application thereunder are the averments in the plaint. The trial Court can exercise the power at any stage of the suit - before registering the plaint or after issuing summons to the defendant at any time before the conclusion of the trial.

IK-1841885:L102.text: For the purposes of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (d) of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are the germane; the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.

IK-1841885:L103.text: In cite18†I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal and Ors. (1998 (2) SCC 70) it was held that the basic question to be decided while dealing with an application filed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code is whether a real cause of action has been set out in the plaint or something purely illusory has been stated with a view to get out of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code.

IK-1841885:L104.text: The trial Court must remember that if on a meaningful and not formal reading of the plaint it is manifestly vexatious and meritless in the sense of not disclosing a clear right to sue, it should exercise the power under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code taking care to see that the ground mentioned therein is fulfilled. If clever drafting has created the illusion of a cause of action, it has to be nipped in the bud at the first hearing by examining the party searchingly under Order X of the Code. (See cite19†T.

IK-1841885:L105.text: Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal and Anr. (1977 (4) SCC 467) It is trite law that not any particular plea has to be considered, and the whole plaint has to be read. As was observed by this Court in cite20†Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill (1982 (3) SCC 487), only a part of the plaint cannot be rejected and if no cause of action is disclosed, the plaint as a whole must be rejected.

IK-1841885:L106.text: In Raptakos Brett & Co.Ltd. v. Ganesh Property (1998 (7) SCC 184) it was observed that the averments in the plaint as a whole have to be seen to find out whether clause

IK-1841885:L108.text: (d) of Rule 11 of Order VII was applicable.

IK-1841885:L109.text: There cannot be any compartmentalization, dissection, segregation and inversions of the language of various paragraphs in the plaint. If such a course is adopted it would run counter to the cardinal canon of interpretation according to which a pleading has to be read as a whole to ascertain its true import. It is not permissible to cull out a sentence or a passage and to read it out of the context in isolation.

IK-1841885:L110.text: Although it is the substance and not merely the form that has to be looked into, the pleading has to be construed as it stands without addition or subtraction or words or change of its apparent grammatical sense. The intention of the party concerned is to be gathered primarily from the tenor and terms of his pleadings taken as a whole. At the same time it should be borne in mind that no pedantic approach should be adopted to defeat justice on hair- splitting technicalities.

IK-1841885:L111.text: Submission of learned counsel for respondent No.2- trust was that requirement of law being reading the plaint in its totality, the appellants cannot take the plea that they would give up or relinquish some of the reliefs sought for. That would not be permissible. The plea clearly overlooks the basic distinction between statements of the facts disclosing cause of action and the reliefs sought for. The reliefs claimed do not constitute the cause of action.

IK-1841885:L112.text: On the contrary, they constitute the entitlement, if any, on the basis of pleaded facts. As indicated above, Order VI Rule 2 requires that pleadings shall contain and contain only a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim. If the plea of Mr. Savant, learned counsel for the respondent-trust is accepted the distinction between the statement of material facts and the reliance on them for the claim shall be obliterated.

IK-1841885:L113.text: What is required in law is not the piecemeal reading of the plaint but in its entirety. Whether the reliefs would be granted on the pleaded facts and the evidence adduced is totally different from the relief claimed. All the reliefs claimed may not be allowed to a party on the pleadings and the evidence adduced.

IK-1841885:L114.text: Whether part of the relief cannot be granted by the Civil Court is a different matter from saying that because of a combined claim of reliefs the jurisdiction is ousted or no cause of action is disclosed. Considering the reliefs claimed vis-a- vis the pleadings would not mean compartmentalization or segregation, in that sense. The plea raised by the respondent-trust is therefore clearly unacceptable.

IK-1841885:L115.text: Keeping in view the aforesaid principles the reliefs sought for in the suit as quoted supra have to be considered. The real object of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code is to keep out of courts irresponsible law suits.

IK-1841885:L116.text: Therefore, the Order X of the Code is a tool in the hands of the Courts by resorting to which and by searching examination of the party in case the Court is prima facie of the view that the suit is an abuse of the process of the court in the sense that it is a bogus and irresponsible litigation, the jurisdiction under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code can be exercised.

IK-1841885:L117.text: As noted supra, the Order VII Rule 11 does not justify rejection of any particular portion of the plaint. Order VI Rule 16 of the Code is relevant in this regard. It deals with 'striking out pleadings'. It has three clauses permitting the Court at any stage of the proceeding to strike out or amend any matter in any pleading i.e.

IK-1841885:L118.text: (a) which may be unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or, (b) which may tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the suit, or, (c) which is otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court.

IK-1841885:L119.text: Order VI Rule 2(1) of the Code states the basic and cardinal rule of pleadings and declares that the pleading has to state material facts and not the evidence. It mandates that every pleading shall contain, and contain only, a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim or defence, as the case may be, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved.

IK-1841885:L120.text: There is distinction between 'material facts' and 'particulars'. The words 'material facts' show that the facts necessary to formulate a complete cause of action must be stated. Omission of a single material fact leads to an incomplete cause of action and the statement or plaint becomes bad. The distinction which has been made between 'material facts' and 'particulars' was brought by Scott, L.J. in Bruce v. Odhams Press Ltd. (1936) 1 KB 697 in the following passage :

IK-1841885:L121.text: > The cardinal provision in Rule 4 is that the statement of claim must state the material facts. The word "material" means necessary for the purpose of formulating a complete cause of action; and if any one "material" statement is omitted, the statement of claim is bad; it is "demurrable" in the old phraseology, and in the new is liable to be "struck out" under R.S.C. Order XXV, Rule 4 (see Philipps v. Philipps ((1878) 4 QBD

IK-1841885:L122.text: > 127)); or "a further and better statement of claim" may be ordered under Rule 7.

IK-1841885:L123.text: The function of "particulars" under Rule 6 is quite different. They are not to be used in order to fill material gaps in a demurrable statement of claim - gaps which ought to have been filled by appropriate statements of the various material facts which together constitute the plaintiff's cause of action. The use of particulars is intended to meet a further and quite separate requirement of pleading, imposed in fairness and justice to the defendant.

IK-1841885:L124.text: Their function is to fill in the picture of the plaintiff's cause of action with information sufficiently detailed to put the defendant on his guard as to the case he had to meet and to enable him to prepare for trial.

IK-1841885:L125.text: The dictum of Scott, L.J. in Bruce case (supra) has been quoted with approval by this Court in cite21†Samant N. Balkrishna v. George Fernandez (1969 (3) SCC 238), and the distinction between "material facts" and "particulars" was brought out in the following terms:

IK-1841885:L126.text: > The word 'material' shows that the facts necessary to formulate a complete cause of action must be stated. Omission of a single material fact leads to an incomplete cause of action and the statement of claim becomes bad. The function of particulars is to present as full a picture of the cause of action with such further information in detail as to make the opposite party understand the case he will have to meet.

IK-1841885:L127.text: > Rule 11 of Order VII lays down an independent remedy made available to the defendant to challenge the maintainability of the suit itself, irrespective of his right to contest the same on merits. The law ostensibly does not contemplate at any stage when the objections can be raised, and also does not say in express terms about the filing of a written statement.

IK-1841885:L128.text: Instead, the word 'shall' is used clearly implying thereby that it casts a duty on the Court to perform its obligations in rejecting the plaint when the same is hit by any of the infirmities provided in the four clauses of Rule 11, even without intervention of the defendant. In any event, rejection of the plaint under Rule 11 does not preclude the plaintiffs from presenting a fresh plaint in terms of Rule 13.

IK-1841885:L129.text: According to Mr. Mohta appearing for the appellants, as noted above, the reliefs are separable and merely because some of the reliefs cannot be granted by the Civil Court it would entail an automatic rejection of the old plaint. In fact he submitted that some of the reliefs would be given up by the plaintiffs in the suit itself. It is true as contended by Mr.

IK-1841885:L130.text: Savant learned counsel appearing for the respondent-trust by ingenious drafting a cause of action in the nature of red herrings cannot be brought into judicial arena. But a reading of the reliefs shows that some of them can only be considered by the Civil Court.

IK-1841885:L131.text: Under Order II Rule 1 of the Code which contains provisions of mandatory nature, the requirement is that the plaintiffs are duty bound to claim the entire relief. The suit has to be so framed as to afford ground for final decision upon the subjects in dispute and to prevent further litigation concerning them. Rule 2 further enjoins on the plaintiff to include the whole of the claim which the plaintiff is entitled to make in respect of the cause of action.

IK-1841885:L132.text: If the plaintiff omits to sue or intentionally relinquishes any portion of his claim, it is not permissible for him to sue in respect of the portion so omitted or relinguished afterwards. If the plaintiffs as contended by Mr. Mohta want to relinquish some reliefs prayer in that regard shall be done before the trial Court.

IK-1841885:L133.text: A reading of the plaint and the reliefs along with the contents of the plaint goes to show that the main dispute relates to the question of continuance of tenancy and the period of tenancy. They are in essence unrelated with the other reliefs regarding enquiry into the affairs of the trust. Such enquiries can only be undertaken under cite13†Section 50 of the Act. For instituting the suit of the nature specified in cite13†Section 50 , prior consent of the Charity Commissioner is necessary under cite14†Section 51 .

IK-1841885:L134.text: To that extent Mr. Savant is right that the reliefs relatable to cite13†Section 50 would require a prior consent in terms of cite14†Section 51 . If the plaintiffs give up those reliefs claimed in accordance with law, the question would be whether a cause of action for the residual claims/reliefs warrant continuance of the suit. The nature of the dispute is to be resolved by the Civil Court. The question of tenancy cannot be decided under cite13†Section 50 of the Act.

IK-1841885:L135.text: cite14†Section 51 is applicable only to suits which are filed by a person having interest in the trust. A tenant of the trust does not fall within the category of a person having an interest in the trust. Except relief in Para D of the plaint, the other reliefs could be claimed before and can be considered and adjudicated by the Civil Courts and the bar or impediment in cite13†Sections 50 and cite14†51 of the Act will have no relevance or application to the other reliefs.

IK-1841885:L136.text: That being so, cite13†Sections 50 and cite14†51 of the Act would not have any application to that part of the relief which relates to question of tenancy, the term of tenancy and the period of tenancy. The inevitable conclusion therefore is that Courts below were not justified in directing rejection of the plaint. However, the adjudication in the suit would be restricted to the question of tenancy, terms of tenancy and the period of tenancy only.

IK-1841885:L137.text: For the rest of the reliefs, the plaintiffs shall be permitted within a month from today to make such application as warranted in law for relinquishing and/or giving up claim for other reliefs.

IK-1841885:L138.text: Another plea which has been raised with some amount of vehemence by the appellant is the alleged forcible possession. This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust who says that the possession was taken in accordance with law and as noted above, by voluntary surrendering by most of the tenants. Much of this controversy revolves from the date till the order of injunction passed by the trial Court operated.

IK-1841885:L139.text: There are two different sets of principles which have to be borne in mind regarding course to be adopted in case of forcible dispossession. Taking up the first aspect, it is true that where a person is in settled possession of property, even on the assumption that he has no right to remain in property, he cannot be disposed by the owner except by recourse of law. This principle is cite21†laid down in cite22†Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

IK-1841885:L140.text: That Section says that if any person is dispossessed without his consent from immovable property other wise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.

IK-1841885:L141.text: That a person without title but in "settled" possession  as against mere fugitive possession  can get back possession if forcibly dispossessed or rather, if dispossessed otherwise than by due process of law, has been cite21†laid down in several cases. It was so held by this Court in Yashwant Singh v. Jagdish Singh (AIR 1968 SC 620), Krishna Ram Mohate v. Mrs. Shobha Venkata Rao, (1989 (4) SCC 131,at p.136), Ram Rattan v. State of U.P. (cite23†1977 (1) SCC 188), and State of U.P. v.

IK-1841885:L142.text: Maharaja Dharmender Prasad Singh (1989 (2) SCC 505). The leading decision quoted in these rulings is the decision of the Bombay High Court in cite24†K.K. Verma v. Union of India (AIR 1954 Bom. 358).

IK-1841885:L143.text: Now the other aspect of the matter needs to be noted.

IK-1841885:L144.text: Assuming a trespasser ousted can seek restoration of possession under cite22†Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 can the trespasser seek injunction against the true owner? This question does not entirely depend upon cite22†Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, but mainly depends upon certain general principles applicable to the law of injunctions and as to the scope of the exercise of discretion while granting injunction? In cite25†Mahadeo Savlaram Sheike v.

IK-1841885:L145.text: Pune Municipal Corporation (1995 (3) SCC 33), it was held, after referring to Woodrofe on "Law relating to injunction; L.C. Goyal 'Law of injunctions; David Bean 'Injunction' Jayce on Injunctions and other leading Articles on the subject that the appellant who was a trespasser in possession could not seek injunction against the true owner. In that context this Court quoted cite26†Shiv Kumar Chadha v. MCD (1993 (3) SCC 161) wherein it was observed that injunction is discretionary and that:

IK-1841885:L146.text: > "Judicial proceedings cannot be used to protect or to perpetuate a wrong committed by a person who approaches the Court".

IK-1841885:L148.text: Reference was also made to cite27†Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh (1992 (1) SCC 719) in regard to the meaning of the words 'prima facie case' and 'balance of convenience' and observed in cite25†Mahadeo 's case (supra) that:

IK-1841885:L150.text: > "It is settled law that no injunction could be granted against the owner at the instance of a person in unlawful possession."

IK-1841885:L151.text: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.

IK-1841885:L152.text: Learned counsel for the respondent-trust has urged with some amount of vehemence about the conduct of the plaintiffs in not depositing the arrears of money and the effect of 22 of the tenants out of total 44 tenants surrendering possession. This is a matter which can be considered in the trial itself so far as it is relevant. It was submitted by learned counsel for the trust that in any event the District Court was the only Court having jurisdiction and not the Court where the suit was filed.

IK-1841885:L153.text: This aspect does not appear to have been specifically urged before the Courts below. So we do not think it appropriate to express our opinion thereon. As regards the question of arrears it shall be open to the respondent-trust to move the trial Court for such directions as are available in law. Looking into the nature of dispute it would be appropriate if the trial Court makes an effort to complete the trial within six months from the date of the judgment.

IK-1841885:L154.text: The parties are directed to cooperate for disposal of the suit early within the stipulated time. The appeal is allowed to the extent indicated without any order as to costs.

limitations: TRUE means the challenge was made, not that rejection was legally justified.
The application was directed against the identified plaint, not independently against each prayer.

P02.text: The plaintiffs filed Regular Civil Suit No. 160 of 1997, asserting a tenancy relationship with the respondent trust and requesting a tenancy declaration, restraint against forcible eviction and interference, compensation, and an inquiry into alleged trust misconduct. This was the plaint subjected to Rule 11 screening.
P02.speaker: Supreme Court describing the plaint and its prayers
P02.quote: The suit was numbered as R.C.S. No.160/1997 in the trial Court.
limitations: The existence and content of the plaint are established as procedural facts.
Its material allegations are not treated as proven.
The distinct trust-inquiry request is separately identified in P09.

P03.text: The plaintiffs claimed to be tenants of Shaneshwar Deosthan Trust and alleged that their tenancy continued notwithstanding the asserted eviction. The judgment records this position without establishing the existence or continuing validity of the tenancy.
P03.time_scope: Claimed continuation at the time of the disputed loss of possession; exact dates not supplied.
P03.speaker: Plaintiffs-appellants, as reported by the Supreme Court
P03.quote: Plaintiffs claimed that they were tenants of the trust
limitations: TRUE applies to the attribution of the claim.
The court did not determine whether the plaintiffs were continuing tenants at the disputed time.
No lease commencement or expiration date is established.

P04.text: The plaintiffs-appellants asserted that the relevant tenancy was for 11 years rather than 11 months.
P04.time_scope: Disputed contractual duration of 11 years; commencement and ending dates not supplied.
P04.speaker: Plaintiffs-appellants
P04.quote: the tenancy was for a period of 11 years and not for 11 months as claimed by the trust.
limitations: TRUE establishes that the 11-year position was asserted.
No finding establishes an 11-year tenancy.
The source does not independently provide the relevant lease instrument.

P05.text: The respondent trust maintained that the tenancy period was 11 months, contrary to the plaintiffs' asserted 11-year period.
P05.time_scope: Disputed contractual duration of 11 months; commencement and ending dates not supplied.
P05.speaker: Respondent trust, as reported by the Supreme Court
P05.quote: not for 11 months as claimed by the trust.
limitations: TRUE establishes attribution of the competing 11-month position.
The Supreme Court did not determine the actual tenancy term.
The disagreement over contractual duration remains distinct from the procedural maintainability question.

P06.text: Prayer A requested a declaration that plaintiffs Nos. 1 to 17 were tenants of the properties described in the plaint as belonging to the temple trust.
P06.time_scope: Prayer in Regular Civil Suit No. 160 of 1997.
P06.speaker: Plaintiffs, through prayer A of the plaint
P06.quote: Plaintiff no. 1 to 17, be declared as the tenants
limitations: The requested declaration does not establish that the plaintiffs were tenants.
A prayer for relief is not itself a material fact constituting a cause of action.

P07.text: Prayer B requested a permanent injunction against forcible eviction, interference with business, and interference with possession of the suit shops. The quoted prayer specifically referred to plaintiffs Nos. 1 to 13.
P07.time_scope: Prayer in Regular Civil Suit No. 160 of 1997.
P07.speaker: Plaintiffs, through prayer B of the plaint
P07.quote: be permanently restrained by an order of injunction not to evict
limitations: The requested injunction is not evidence that forcible eviction occurred.
The requested relief does not establish settled possession or equitable entitlement.
The source's different plaintiff-number ranges must not be silently equated.

P08.text: Prayer C requested compensation from the trust-side defendants for alleged losses resulting from acts or omissions before the filing of the suit and possible damage during its pendency.
P08.time_scope: Alleged loss before institution of the suit and prospective damage during the suit.
P08.speaker: Plaintiffs, through prayer C of the plaint
P08.quote: to pay compensation for the loss caused to the plaintiffs
limitations: The existence of a compensation request does not establish loss, causation, or liability.
The Supreme Court's restriction of continued adjudication must not be interpreted as an award of compensation.

P09.text: Prayer D requested that defendant No. 1, the Assistant Charity Commissioner, inquire into allegedly illegal acts attributed to the trust and its trustees and issue appropriate directions. The alleged misconduct was not established by the inclusion of this prayer.
P09.time_scope: Prayer in Regular Civil Suit No. 160 of 1997.
P09.speaker: Plaintiffs, through prayer D of the plaint
P09.quote: be directed to enquire into the illegal acts
limitations: TRUE records the prayer, not the occurrence of illegal acts.
The Commissioner is the proposed investigating authority, not the trust or the alleged wrongdoer.
The trust-affairs inquiry is distinct from the contested tenancy transaction.

P10.text: The trust argued that the plaint disclosed no cause of action and that Sections 50, 51 and 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act prevented ordinary civil-court consideration of the requested reliefs. It also advanced the position that the District Court was the competent forum for directions to the Commissioner.
P10.time_scope: Rule 11 proceedings and subsequent appellate arguments.
P10.speaker: Respondent trust and its counsel
P10.quote: no Civil court had jurisdiction to decide or deal with any question
limitations: TRUE means the statutory-bar and jurisdiction objections were asserted.
The applicability of those objections is not established by the submissions.
The separate District-Court-only objection was not decided by the Supreme Court.

P11.text: The trial court found that the plaint disclosed no cause of action and accepted objections based on the Public Trusts Act and civil-court jurisdiction, rejecting the plaint. The first appellate District Court affirmed the trial decree, and the High Court upheld the lower conclusions in second appeal.
P11.time_scope: Trial decree dated 2000-10-21; subsequent first appeal and second appeal before Supreme Court review.
P11.speaker: Trial court, first appellate District Court and High Court, as reported by the Supreme Court
P11.quote: A finding was recorded that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action
limitations: TRUE records the lower-court determinations and appellate affirmances.
Those determinations are not treated as Supreme Court-approved conclusions.
The later Supreme Court reasoning rejected the justification for rejecting the entire plaint.

P12.text: The respondent trust argued that the plaintiffs had not approached the court with clean hands, had pursued an earlier Article 226 writ proceeding, failed to comply with High Court interim directions concerning deposits, and adopted improper litigation methods. Trust counsel also raised alleged arrears and potential financial loss.
P12.time_scope: Earlier writ proceeding and related events before or during the civil suit; precise dates not supplied.
P12.speaker: Counsel for the respondent trust
P12.quote: the plaintiffs have not approached the Court with clean hands.
limitations: TRUE applies only to the recorded trust-side allegations.
The supplied judgment does not independently authenticate deposit records or establish deliberate misconduct.
The Supreme Court left relevant arrears and conduct matters for appropriate trial-court consideration.
The submissions do not displace the plaint-focused Rule 11 screening method.

P13.text: The Supreme Court stated that Rule 11(a) and (d) screening examines the plaint's own averments, understood meaningfully and as a whole, rather than the defendant's rebuttal. Pleaded material facts must be distinguished from requested reliefs, and an illusory or manifestly vexatious cause of action remains vulnerable to Rule 11.
P13.speaker: Supreme Court adopting and applying the stated Rule 11 screening principles
P13.quote: the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.
limitations: This is the applicable screening framework, not an independent finding that every pleaded fact is true.
A meaningful whole-plaint inquiry can still result in rejection when a prescribed ground is established.
Failure to plead a necessary material fact cannot be repaired merely by particulars.
Rule 11 does not authorize partial rejection of a plaint; striking out matter under Order VI Rule 16 is distinct.

P14.text: After considering the plaint and requested reliefs together, the Supreme Court characterized the principal controversy as the continuance and period of the alleged tenancy. The separate prayer for investigation into trust affairs was identified as essentially unrelated to that tenancy controversy.
P14.time_scope: Characterization of the dispute pleaded in Regular Civil Suit No. 160 of 1997.
P14.speaker: Supreme Court
P14.quote: the main dispute relates to the question of continuance of tenancy and the period of tenancy.
limitations: This finding identifies the substantive subject of the pleading.
It is not a finding that the alleged 11-year tenancy existed.
It does not determine that the plaintiffs retained tenancy rights at the disputed time.
The tenancy transaction and the trust-affairs inquiry remain distinct.

P15.text: The Supreme Court distinguished adjudication of tenancy existence, continuation, terms and duration from statutory inquiries into trust affairs. It held that the tenancy controversy was a subject for civil-court determination and was not displaced by Sections 50 and 51 merely because the alleged landlord was a public trust.
P15.speaker: Supreme Court
P15.quote: The nature of the dispute is to be resolved by the Civil Court.
limitations: TRUE concerns suitability for civil adjudication of the tenancy subject.
The Supreme Court did not decide the substantive existence, duration or enforceability of the tenancy.
The particular District-Court-only forum objection was expressly left undecided.
The rule does not independently resolve every conceivable Section 80 jurisdictional issue.

P16.text: The Supreme Court classified the separate request to investigate trust affairs as a matter governed by Section 50 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act and stated that prior Charity Commissioner consent is required under Section 51 for institution of suits of the nature specified in Section 50. This classification did not transform the tenancy dispute into a trust-affairs inquiry.
P16.speaker: Supreme Court
P16.quote: They are in essence unrelated with the other reliefs regarding enquiry into the affairs of the trust.
limitations: The Section 51 consent discussion concerns suits of the nature specified in Section 50.
The judgment states that a tenant is not, merely by that status, a person having an interest in the trust for Section 51.
The source establishes neither a completed consent application nor the absence of consent.
The source does not establish illegal conduct by the trust or trustees.

P17.text: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that combining a civil-adjudicable tenancy controversy with prayers potentially governed by the Public Trusts Act necessarily destroys the entire plaint. It distinguished the material facts comprising a cause of action from the reliefs requested on those facts, while preserving the prohibition on partial rejection under Rule 11 and the possibility of separate lawful procedural treatment of other prayers.
P17.speaker: Supreme Court
P17.quote: The reliefs claimed do not constitute the cause of action.
limitations: The mere combination of reliefs is not itself a sufficient reason to reject the whole plaint.
The proposition does not establish that every independently defective plaint must survive.
It does not authorize rejection of only selected paragraphs or prayers under Rule 11.
It does not establish that the plaintiffs will obtain any of their requested substantive reliefs.
The adequacy of residual claims and lawful relinquishment procedures remain distinct questions.

P18.text: The Supreme Court stated that continued adjudication of the suit would be confined to the tenancy, its terms and its duration. This is recorded as the target court's procedural determination, not as evidence establishing the truth of any tenancy allegation or as a premise from which the rejection decision is independently proved.
P18.speaker: Supreme Court
P18.quote: the adjudication in the suit would be restricted to the question of tenancy, terms of tenancy and the period of tenancy only.
limitations: This records the scope of continued proceedings.
It is not evidence of an established 11-year tenancy or an established right to remain in possession.
It does not itself grant injunction, restoration or compensation.
It must not be used circularly to prove the procedural reasoning that led to the restriction.

P19.text: The Supreme Court permitted the plaintiffs to make an appropriate application within one month for relinquishing or giving up other reliefs. Its reasoning separately noted the Order II provisions concerning complete claims and consequences of omitted or intentionally relinquished claims.
P19.time_scope: One-month period measured from the Supreme Court judgment dated 2004-01-23.
P19.speaker: Supreme Court
P19.quote: the plaintiffs shall be permitted within a month from today to make such application as warranted in law
limitations: Permission to apply does not establish that an application was subsequently made.
It does not establish that any proposed relinquishment was accepted.
The source does not resolve future consequences of an actual relinquishment.
This procedural direction is not a merits determination.

P20.text: The plaintiffs alleged that they were forcibly evicted from the trust's properties despite the asserted continuation of their tenancy. Their counsel also argued that a person in settled possession could obtain protection against dispossession outside due process of law.
P20.speaker: Plaintiffs-appellants and their counsel
P20.quote: Alleging that they have been forcibly evicted notwithstanding continuance of the tenancy
limitations: TRUE confirms the existence of the allegation, not the occurrence of unlawful eviction.
No specific dispossession date is supplied.
The allegation does not independently establish prior settled possession, lack of consent, or absence of lawful process.
The trust contested the characterization of the same disputed possession event.

P21.text: The respondent trust disputed the plaintiffs' allegation of forcible eviction and maintained that possession was taken in accordance with law. Its counsel referred to voluntary surrender by most tenants as part of that contrary account.
P21.speaker: Counsel for the respondent trust
P21.quote: the possession was taken in accordance with law
limitations: TRUE records the respondent's denial and affirmative characterization.
The judgment does not independently establish lawful process or consent by the identified plaintiffs.
Voluntary surrender by unidentified other tenants cannot automatically be attributed to these plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs' disputed event is not split into separate events merely because the parties describe it differently.

P22.speaker: Counsel for the respondent trust
P22.quote: the effect of 22 of the tenants out of total 44 tenants surrendering possession.
limitations: TRUE records the numerical submission, not independently verified surrender events.
The identity of the 22 tenants is unknown.
No evidentiary basis permits identifying the group as the plaintiffs or inferring voluntary surrender by a particular plaintiff.
The other tenants' asserted surrenders must not be merged into the disputed taking of possession from the identified plaintiffs.

P23.text: The Supreme Court identified the period during which the trial court's injunction operated as a significant aspect of the disagreement over possession. The supplied judgment does not establish the dates necessary to settle that issue.
P23.speaker: Supreme Court
P23.quote: Much of this controversy revolves from the date till the order of injunction passed by the trial Court operated.
limitations: TRUE establishes that the court identified the injunction period as material.
It does not establish when the injunction commenced or ceased.
It does not establish when any plaintiff lost possession.
No valid temporal ordering between the injunction and the disputed taking of possession can be reconstructed.

P24.text: The supplied judgment does not determine whether the identified plaintiffs actually held settled possession of the suit shops, as distinct from mere fugitive possession, at the time relevant to the alleged dispossession.
P24.speaker: No plaintiff-specific evidentiary determination supplied; Supreme Court reserved the possession controversy
P24.quote: We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.
limitations: UNKNOWN must not be converted to FALSE because possession evidence is absent.
General statements about legal protection of settled possession do not establish that these plaintiffs satisfied the factual condition.
No independently examined possession documents, witness testimony or possession dates are supplied.

P25.text: The plaintiffs asserted forcible and unlawful dispossession while the trust denied forcible ouster and maintained that possession was lawfully taken. The judgment does not resolve whether the identified plaintiffs were dispossessed without consent otherwise than through due process of law.
P25.speaker: Opposing submissions of plaintiffs-appellants and respondent trust, recorded by the Supreme Court
P25.quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust
limitations: CONFLICTED represents competing party accounts rather than a judicial finding resolving the factual proposition.
The record does not independently establish consent, lawful process or unlawful force.
The precise identity of persons who surrendered and the relevant possession dates remain unresolved.
The disputed taking of possession is represented as one controversy, not artificially separated according to the speaker.

P26.text: The Supreme Court described the Section 6 principle under which a person dispossessed of immovable property without consent otherwise than in due course of law may seek recovery notwithstanding competing title. It distinguished settled possession from merely fugitive possession.
P26.speaker: Supreme Court
P26.quote: if any person is dispossessed without his consent from immovable property
limitations: This is a legal standard, not evidence that the identified plaintiffs satisfied it.
No actual entitlement to restoration was determined.
Settled possession, identity of the actual possessor, consent and compliance with due process remain factual questions.
Possible recovery under Section 6 is distinct from entitlement to discretionary injunction.

P27.text: The Supreme Court separately discussed injunction principles, including the discretionary nature of injunctions, the relevance of prima facie case and balance of convenience, and the stated restriction against granting an injunction to someone in unlawful possession against the true owner.
P27.speaker: Supreme Court recounting injunction principles
P27.quote: no injunction could be granted against the owner at the instance of a person in unlawful possession.
limitations: The rule is conditional on facts including unlawful possession and true ownership.
The Supreme Court did not determine that these particular plaintiffs were unlawful possessors.
The judgment did not grant or refuse a merits-based injunction on application of these standards to established facts.
Section 6 restoration principles cannot automatically establish discretionary injunction entitlement.

P28.text: No plaintiff-specific merits determination of equitable entitlement to injunction is supplied. The discussion of general injunction principles does not establish the factual conditions for granting or denying an injunction in this suit.
P28.speaker: No plaintiff-specific injunction entitlement determination supplied by the Supreme Court
limitations: UNKNOWN concerns substantive entitlement and its factual prerequisites.
No finding resolves prima facie case, balance of convenience, unlawful possession, or the effect of relevant conduct for these plaintiffs.
The procedural continuation of the tenancy dispute is not a determination that an injunction should issue.
The general prohibition discussed in the judgment is not itself a plaintiff-specific finding against relief.

P29.text: The Supreme Court expressly declined to determine the disputed forcible-possession issue. It stated that the parties could raise the matter before the trial court and that the court should consider its relevance to the continued suit before accepting or rejecting the plea according to law.
P29.time_scope: Supreme Court review dated 2004-01-23; possible subsequent trial-court consideration if raised and relevant.
P29.speaker: Supreme Court
P29.quote: if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit
limitations: TRUE establishes the express reservation of the merits question.
The Supreme Court did not find forcible dispossession proved or disproved.
The trial court was not directed to accept the allegation or to conduct an unrestricted inquiry into every proposed issue.
Potential consideration depends on the issue being raised and found relevant to the continued suit.
The reservation does not determine entitlement to restoration, injunction or compensation.

P30.text: The judgment records two opposing descriptions of the contested possession event: the plaintiffs' allegation of forcible eviction despite continuing tenancy and the trust's denial of forcible eviction coupled with its assertion of lawful taking. The existence of these contrary assertions is established as part of the litigation record, without resolving the underlying event.
P30.speaker: Supreme Court recording competing party submissions
P30.quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust
limitations: TRUE applies to the recording of opposing versions.
It does not mean that both incompatible descriptions of the underlying event are true.
The underlying legality of the dispossession remains conflicted or unresolved.
The trust's assertions about surrender by other tenants do not identify any named plaintiff as a surrendering tenant.

R1@1.description: Order VII Rule 11(a)/(d) is a plaint-focused screening procedure. The court reads the whole plaint meaningfully, considers its material factual averments rather than the defendant's denials, and does not equate a prayer for relief with the facts constituting a cause of action.
R1@1.conclusion_text: A Rule 11(a)/(d) challenge must be screened on the material factual allegations of the plaint as a whole, not by proving or disproving those allegations through the defence or by treating each requested relief as a separate cause of action.
R1@1.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court review of civil procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
R1@1.source_quote: For the purposes of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (d) of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are the germane; the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.

slots.name: rule11_challenge
slots.description: A party has invoked Rule 11(a) or (d) against the identified plaintiffs' plaint; recording the objection does not validate it.

slots.name: plaint_for_review
slots.description: An identified plaint, including its pleaded material facts and prayers, is the object of the screening; its allegations are not yet proven.

scope_limits: This rule prescribes the screening method; it does not find that a particular plaint actually discloses a sufficient cause of action.
A genuinely illusory or manifestly vexatious cause of action may still trigger Rule 11; the whole plaint, not an isolated paragraph, must be assessed.
Rule 11 does not allow rejection of only part of a plaint. Order VI Rule 16 striking out matter is a distinct mechanism.
Cited decisions are available only through this judgment's description of them.
unimplemented: The meaningful, whole-plaint appraisal of omitted material facts, illusory causes, and statutory bars is a semantic judicial evaluation, not an executable checklist.

R2@1.description: A materially pleaded controversy over whether a trust's tenant relationship continued and how long the tenancy lasted is a civil tenancy subject, distinct from administering or investigating the trust under Sections 50 and 51 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act.
R2@1.conclusion_text: Where meaningful reading of the plaint identifies a substantive tenancy-continuance or tenancy-term controversy, those questions are for civil-court adjudication rather than determination as a Section 50 trust-affairs inquiry.
R2@1.jurisdiction: India; Maharashtra trust-tenancy controversy under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, as addressed by the Supreme Court
R2@1.source_quote: The question of tenancy cannot be decided under Section 50 of the Act.

slots.name: plaint_screen_framework
slots.description: The screening must use the whole-plaint method produced by R1, not the truth of the trust's rebuttal.

slots.name: tenancy_dispute_characterization
slots.description: The target court characterizes the principal pleaded controversy as continuation and period of the tenancy; this is not a finding that an 11-year term, rather than an 11-month term, existed.

scope_limits: Only subject-matter suitability for civil tenancy adjudication is addressed; the tenancy's existence, duration, continuing validity, and plaintiffs' ultimate rights are not resolved.
The judgment says a tenant is not, by that status, a person having an interest in the trust for Section 51.
This does not independently decide every possible Section 80 objection or whether a different civil court is the proper forum.
unimplemented: Determining the true substantive subject of a plaint, rather than accepting nominal tenancy wording or clever drafting, remains an OPEN_TEXT assessment.
The competing alleged tenancy lengths and legal effect of any lease documentation are not adjudicated here.

R3@1.description: A prayer to direct an inquiry into allegedly improper affairs of a public trust follows the distinct Section 50 trust-affairs route; the judgment describes prior Charity Commissioner consent under Section 51 for institution of a suit of the type specified in Section 50.
R3@1.conclusion_text: A genuine trust-affairs inquiry prayer is treated under Section 50 and the applicable Section 51 consent regime rather than being converted into an ordinary tenancy question.
R3@1.jurisdiction: India; Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, as applied in the Maharashtra civil proceeding reviewed by the Supreme Court
R3@1.source_quote: Such enquiries can only be undertaken under Section 50 of the Act.

slots.name: trust_affairs_prayer
slots.description: The plaint includes a separate prayer that the Commissioner inquire into alleged illegal acts by the trust and trustees; this records a requested remedy, not proof of illegal acts.

scope_limits: Section 51's prior-consent requirement is described for suits of the nature specified in Section 50; it is not imposed on every dispute with a trust.
The Commissioner who is asked to inquire is not the trust or its trustees, and the trust inquiry is not the same transaction as the tenancy.
The judgment does not supply proof of either a consent application or consent's absence, and it does not establish trust misconduct.
unimplemented: Whether a differently worded relief truly falls within Section 50, and any applicable consent facts, require case-specific examination.

R4@1.description: Separation of pleaded material facts from requested reliefs prevents a trust-affairs prayer from automatically destroying the separate tenancy cause. Rule 11 cannot reject just one portion of a plaint, but a claimant who wants to relinquish some prayers must seek the appropriate order at trial, with Order II claim consequences kept distinct.
R4@1.conclusion_text: When a whole-plaint review identifies a civil-adjudicable tenancy subject alongside a separate special-Act trust-inquiry prayer, the mere combination of those prayers does not itself justify rejecting the entire plaint; lawful restriction to tenancy issues and applications to relinquish other prayers are distinct procedural matters.
R4@1.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court review of Rule 11 rejection in a Maharashtra trust-tenancy civil suit
R4@1.source_quote: Whether part of the relief cannot be granted by the Civil Court is a different matter from saying that because of a combined claim of reliefs the jurisdiction is ousted or no cause of action is disclosed.

slots.name: holistic_gatekeeping
slots.description: Use R1's full-plaint, material-facts screening framework.

slots.name: civil_tenancy_track
slots.description: R2 has identified tenancy subject matter available for civil adjudication without deciding the tenant's merits.

slots.name: distinct_trust_inquiry_track
slots.description: R3 identifies the separate inquiry prayer; its transaction must remain distinct from the tenancy transaction.

scope_limits: This is a non-entailment rule: mixing prayers is not itself a sufficient Rule 11(a)/(d) ground. It does not immunize an otherwise defective plaint.
Only rejection of the whole plaint is tested here; partial rejection under Rule 11 is not authorized.
A relinquishment request must be addressed to the trial court under the applicable rules; Order II Rules 1 and 2 address claims omitted or intentionally relinquished.

The target court ultimately restricted adjudication to tenancy, tenancy terms and period, despite noting other civil-court-considerable prayers; this registry does not convert those prayers into granted relief.
unimplemented: The adequacy of the residual tenancy cause and any independent whole-plaint ground for rejection require the OPEN_TEXT appraisal from R2 and R1.
Whether and how other reliefs are legally relinquished requires a trial-court application; none is evidenced as completed by this judgment.

R5@1.description: Opposing party assertions about an asserted eviction are recorded as opposing versions only. The presence of the two statements is different from establishing which account of possession is correct.
R5@1.conclusion_text: The litigants advance contrary versions of the identified dispossession, without that record itself proving a forcible ouster, voluntary surrender by the same plaintiffs, or lawful taking of possession.
R5@1.jurisdiction: India; evidentiary-role reconstruction of the Maharashtra civil plaint as reported in Supreme Court review
R5@1.source_quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust who says that the possession was taken in accordance with law and as noted above, by voluntary surrendering by most of the tenants.

slots.name: claimants_ouster_allegation_recorded
slots.description: It is recorded that the plaintiffs alleged forcible eviction despite claimed continuing tenancy, without adopting the alleged event as a finding.

slots.name: trust_denial_recorded
slots.description: The trust disputes forcible dispossession and claims lawful taking; the stated surrender by most tenants cannot be attributed to any named plaintiff without identification.

scope_limits: TRUE applies to the recording of both assertions, not to the truth of either description of dispossession.
The judgment reports surrender by 22 of 44 tenants as a trust-counsel point; it does not identify the surrenders as the plaintiffs' acts.
The court notes controversy surrounding how long the trial court injunction operated; no chronology sufficient to resolve the merits is supplied.
unimplemented: No underlying possession documents, testimony, surrender instruments, or dates are independently available to establish whose account is accurate.

R6@1.description: Continuation of an adjudicable tenancy issue is analytically separate from proving dispossession and from injunction discretion. The judgment describes Section 6 recovery for loss of settled possession without consent otherwise than by due course of law, but also recounts the rule that unlawful possession cannot be protected against the true owner by injunction; discretionary factors require separate assessment.
R6@1.conclusion_text: Procedural survival of the tenancy issue cannot itself establish forcible dispossession, a right to Section 6 recovery, or entitlement to injunction; relevant evidence and discretionary injunction standards must be assessed separately in the appropriate trial proceedings.
R6@1.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court civil plaint-rejection review discussing Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and injunction principles
R6@1.source_quote: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.

slots.name: surviving_tenancy_track
slots.description: R4's procedural non-rejection conclusion addresses the tenancy track, not possession relief.

slots.name: opposed_dispossession_versions
slots.description: R5 establishes that opposite accounts were asserted, not that either alleged event was proved.

slots.name: settled_possession_proof
slots.description: Whether the identified plaintiffs actually held settled rather than fugitive possession is not determined in this review.

slots.name: unlawful_dispossession_proof
slots.description: The plaintiffs' allegations and trust's contrary version conflict; the full nonconsensual and unlawful dispossession proposition is not decided. Timing relative to the trial injunction is material.

slots.name: injunction_discretion_merits
slots.description: Lawfulness of possession as against the true owner, prima facie case, balance of convenience, and any relevant conduct have not been decided as an injunction entitlement determination.

scope_limits: Section 6 restoration and discretionary injunction are different questions: possible recovery despite lack of title does not itself justify injunction against a true owner.

The judgment recounts a rule against injunction for a person in unlawful possession against the true owner, but does not find that these specific plaintiffs were unlawful possessors or that an injunction is due or barred on their merits.
The Supreme Court expressly leaves forcible-dispossession issues to the trial court if raised and relevant, and offers no view on the merits.
Claims about arrears, compliance with prior High Court orders, and surrender by other tenants are trust-side submissions or matters left for trial; their significance cannot be presumed.

No judgment-stage finding or supplied primary evidence resolves plaintiffs' claimed eviction; unknown and conflicted propositions cannot be promoted to either TRUE or FALSE by the procedural ruling.

R6@2.description: Recorded procedural tenancy route and express reservation of merits do not decide those reserved merits.
R6@2.conclusion_text: Continuation of the tenancy issue does not decide the reserved possession or injunction merits; a forcible-possession plea may be raised and considered only insofar as relevant to the continued suit.
R6@2.jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court civil plaint-rejection review discussing Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and injunction principles
R6@2.source_quote: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.

slots.description: R4's procedural non-rejection conclusion addresses the tenancy track, not possession relief.

slots.description: The court expressly declines a merits view and leaves a plea to trial only if raised and relevant.

scope_limits: Restricted to this judgment-stage reconstruction. Relevant pleas may be accepted or rejected; no mandatory full merits adjudication of every claim is inferred.

web_review.quote: For the purposes of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (d) of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are the germane; the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.
web_review.reason: The rule faithfully translates the judgment's Order VII Rule 11(a)/(d) screening method. The trust's recorded challenge and the identified plaint are appropriate procedural premises. Their ALL connective establishes the context in which the screening method applies, without establishing that the challenge succeeds. The conclusion correctly requires meaningful consideration of the plaint as a whole, distinguishes material factual averments from requested reliefs, and excludes the defendant's factual rebuttal from the initial screening assessment. The conclusion does not improperly establish that this particular plaint discloses a sufficient cause of action. The scope limits appropriately preserve rejection where a meaningful reading reveals an illusory or manifestly vexatious cause of action, and distinguish rejection of the entire plaint from striking out particular pleading matter under Order VI Rule 16. The judgment additionally emphasizes that omission of a necessary material fact can leave a cause of action incomplete, that a statutory bar must appear from the plaint for clause (d), and that Rule 11 imposes a duty to reject where its conditions are satisfied. These considerations are compatible with the rule's screening framework and its identified unimplemented semantic evaluation. NOT_COVERED is an appropriate burden policy because the supplied judgment does not establish a comprehensive evidentiary burden allocation for this reconstruction.

web_review.quote: The nature of the dispute is to be resolved by the Civil Court. The question of tenancy cannot be decided under Section 50 of the Act.
web_review.reason: The conclusion is faithful to the Supreme Court's characterization of the substantive controversy as the continuance, terms, and period of the tenancy, rather than an inquiry into the administration of the public trust. The rule appropriately consumes R1's screening framework and the target court's recorded characterization of the dispute. Its OPEN_TEXT connective is justified because determining the true substantive subject of a plaint requires interpretation of its material allegations and cannot be reduced to detecting tenancy terminology. The conclusion establishes civil adjudicability of the tenancy subject, not the existence of an eleven-year lease, the invalidity of an eleven-month lease, or the plaintiffs' ultimate entitlement to relief. The rule also correctly preserves the judgment's distinction between a trust tenant and a person having an interest in the trust for Section 51 purposes. Its scope does not generalize the Supreme Court's analysis into a complete determination of every Section 80 jurisdictional objection or the separate contention concerning the District Court's exclusive jurisdiction. Those limitations are important because the trial court and appellate courts had accepted jurisdictional objections, while the Supreme Court expressly declined to decide the separate District Court objection. No unsupported evidentiary burden is assigned.

web_review.quote: Such enquiries can only be undertaken under Section 50 of the Act. For instituting the suit of the nature specified in Section 50, prior consent of the Charity Commissioner is necessary under Section 51.
web_review.reason: The rule accurately preserves the distinct statutory treatment of the plaint's request to direct an inquiry into alleged illegal acts involving the trust and its trustees. Its single recorded-prayer premise establishes that the particular relief was requested, without establishing misconduct. The ALL connective is acceptable for this narrowly identified prayer; it does not purport to classify every conceivable trust-related relief automatically. The conclusion is supported by the judgment's express treatment of inquiries into trust affairs under Section 50 and its description of prior consent under Section 51 for suits of the nature specified in Section 50. Importantly, the rule does not convert those provisions into a general prohibition against civil tenancy litigation involving a trust. Its limitations correctly distinguish the Commissioner from the trust and trustees, acknowledge that the inquiry transaction is separate from the tenancy transaction, and avoid inferring either the presence or the absence of statutory consent without supporting evidence. The necessary case-specific assessment of differently formulated reliefs is expressly unimplemented. The judgment supplies no additional burden allocation requiring incorporation.

web_review.quote: Whether part of the relief cannot be granted by the Civil Court is a different matter from saying that because of a combined claim of reliefs the jurisdiction is ousted or no cause of action is disclosed.
web_review.reason: This rule faithfully translates the judgment's distinction between a defective cause of action and a plaint combining reliefs subject to different legal regimes. Its three premises appropriately connect the whole-plaint screening method, the civil-adjudicable tenancy controversy, and the separate trust-affairs inquiry route. The ALL connective is suitable for the narrow mixed-relief configuration addressed here. The conclusion is carefully limited to the proposition that combining those reliefs is not, by itself, sufficient to justify rejection of the entire plaint. It does not assert that every residual tenancy cause is adequate, that every claimed relief can be granted, or that Rule 11 permits partial rejection. The scope correctly distinguishes Order VII Rule 11 from Order VI Rule 16 and recognizes the separate procedural treatment of relinquished claims under Order II Rules 1 and 2. It also preserves the need for an appropriate trial-court application where relinquishment is sought, without treating the contemplated application as already made or granted. The Supreme Court's restriction of adjudication to tenancy, its terms, and its period is consistent with this narrow non-entailment rule. Independent reasons for rejecting a plaint remain subject to meaningful appraisal, as the unimplemented limitations acknowledge. The burden policy does not introduce unsupported requirements.

web_review.quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust who says that the possession was taken in accordance with law and as noted above, by voluntary surrendering by most of the tenants.
web_review.reason: The rule accurately reconstructs the presence of competing litigant assertions without deciding the underlying dispossession question. The plaintiffs' allegation of forcible eviction notwithstanding claimed continuing tenancy and the trust's contrary account of lawful possession-taking are expressly reported in the judgment. The ALL connective is suitable because the conclusion concerns the recorded coexistence of those opposing versions. The proposition established is that the assertions were advanced, not that either account is true. The rule properly avoids attributing voluntary surrender to the identified plaintiffs merely because trust counsel referred to surrender by most tenants or to 22 out of 44 tenants. Those reported descriptions do not independently identify the tenants involved, and the judgment does not establish the alleged surrenders through primary evidence. The rule also preserves the unresolved controversy concerning the duration of the trial court injunction and its possible significance for possession. It does not treat the Supreme Court's account of counsel submissions as independent documentary or testimonial proof. The evidentiary question remains unresolved, and the NOT_COVERED burden policy is appropriate.

web_review.quote: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.
web_review.reason: The central legal distinction is supported: survival of the tenancy controversy through plaint-rejection review does not itself prove forcible dispossession, establish a right to recover possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, or establish entitlement to a discretionary injunction. The judgment separately describes protection of settled possession against dispossession otherwise than by due process and the limitation on injunctions sought by persons in unlawful possession against true owners. It does not decide that either description applies to these plaintiffs. The rule also correctly identifies the importance of possession evidence, the opposing accounts, and injunction discretion. However, its premise structure and conclusion strength require correction before acceptance. The OPEN_TEXT rule makes specific UNKNOWN and CONFLICTED evidentiary states mandatory inputs to a non-entailment proposition that does not logically depend on those states. Procedural continuation would not itself establish the possession or injunction merits even if those issues were later established through independent evidence. Conversely, conflicting accounts are not necessary for the procedural-versus-merits distinction to apply. The predicate INJUNCTION_EQUITABLE_ENTITLEMENT_ADJUDICATED also requires careful separation of an expressly absent Supreme Court merits determination from uncertainty about the underlying entitlement or possible earlier interlocutory determinations. More importantly, the conclusion's statement that relevant evidence and discretionary injunction standards must be assessed in trial proceedings risks imposing a broader mandatory merits determination than the judgment directs. The Supreme Court restricted adjudication in the continuing suit to tenancy, its terms, and its period. It permitted the forcible-possession plea to be raised and considered only if raised and relevant to that suit, and expressed no opinion on its merits. The judgment did not independently order adjudication of an injunction entitlement claim. The rule's scope limits partially recognize these qualifications but do not cure the stronger operative wording or unnecessary status-dependent premises. The discretionary injunction evaluation appropriately remains OPEN_TEXT, and no additional evidentiary burden can be supplied from the judgment.
exceptions_or_scope_missing: The operative conclusion must preserve the judgment's qualification that a forcible-possession contention is considered by the trial court only if raised and relevant to the continuing suit.

The operative conclusion must respect the express restriction of continuing adjudication to the tenancy, its terms, and its period; it must not independently mandate a trial determination of injunction entitlement.

The non-entailment of possession and injunction merits from procedural continuation must not depend on settled possession being UNKNOWN, unlawful dispossession being CONFLICTED, or injunction adjudication being UNKNOWN.

The absence of a Supreme Court merits determination must remain distinct from the truth or falsity of the underlying entitlement, and from any incompletely described interlocutory injunction proceedings.
Any eventual Section 6 assessment requires its own applicable possession, consent, and due-process evaluation; it must not be collapsed into discretionary injunction analysis.

The judgment identifies prima facie case, balance of convenience, unlawful possession against a true owner, and judicial discretion as relevant considerations, but does not establish that these factors form an exhaustive conjunctive checklist.
